---
title: "Recipes"
---

Recipes are short task pages. Each recipe solves one task. Each recipe ends with a check you can run.
The recipes rise in difficulty. Recipe 1 installs Trishula on a local Docker provider and reads the first verdict.
The later recipes write rules, read verdict records and tune enforcement. Seven more recipes are planned.

## The recipe ramp

The table lists the planned ramp. Simple tasks sit first. Advanced tasks sit last.
A planned recipe stays PENDING until a worked pin and a smoke run exist.

## The recipe form

Every recipe carries the same parts:

- A header strip table. The columns: Tool, Section, Level, Time, Layer, Tags.
- **Problem** — the task and its walls.
- **Solution** — numbered steps. Each step quotes a real command.
- **Discussion** — what the step did. What to watch. What to tune.
- **See also** — the linked surfaces.
- Expected output shows shapes and placeholders only. A recipe never prints an invented transcript.
- The provenance footer records the pin, the date and the smoke status.

Level is metadata: easy, medium or hard. Level never becomes a navigation layer.
The prose follows [ASD-STE100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Technical_English):

- One thought per sentence. 20 words at most.
- Active voice. Present tense. Approved verbs. Digits for numbers.
- Steps read imperative.

## Recipe 1 — Install Trishula on a kind cluster and see the first verdict

| Tool | Section | Level | Time | Layer | Tags |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [`lab/dx1/`](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/tree/main/lab/dx1) on any Docker provider (kind, or OrbStack Kubernetes) | Getting started | easy | 15 min | gateway + engine | install, kind, verdict |

### Problem

You want Trishula on a local Kubernetes cluster. You want one enforced verdict on one probe request.
You want it inside the 15 min M3 gate window. You do not want a hosted cluster or manual manifests.

### Solution

You need docker, crane, helm, kubectl, go and curl. You need one Docker provider:
kind, or the OrbStack-provided Kubernetes.

1. Clone the product repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula && cd trishula
```

2. Run the timed DX1 gate. The gate builds the linux binaries, brings the lab up
and times the first enforced rule:

```bash
bash lab/dx1/dx1-gate.sh
```

3. Read the printed evidence. The shapes below come from the recorded run.
Volatile values stand as placeholders:

```text
== pre-policy baseline: the benign probe passes transparently (200)
== (d) effect: SQLi probe → 403
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
== M9 apply→effect: <ms> (target ≤ 5s) — PASS
== DX1 verify: hop 1 NGF -> hop 2 engine -> hop 3 echo pod all evidenced above
== Done. The lab remains installed (no teardown).
```

The gate asserts the verdict fields on the blocked probe: `X-Trishula-Decision: block`
and `X-Trishula-Rule: DX-LAB-001`. The probe answers 403.

4. The three legs run alone. Each leg is idempotent. The lab stays installed:

```bash
bash lab/dx1/setup.sh
bash lab/dx1/apply-effect.sh
bash lab/dx1/verify.sh
```

`setup.sh` reuses the cluster, rebuilds the engine image and re-applies the manifests.
`apply-effect.sh` applies the policy, compiles the bundle and times the apply→effect leg.
`verify.sh` prints the hop-by-hop evidence. Re-run any leg at any time.

### Discussion

The request path carries three hops:

```text
client ──> NGF edge-gateway ──> dx1-engine ──> dx1-echo
```

The engine hop marks its response with `X-Trishula-Hop: engine`.
A second Host value on the same NodePort skips the engine. The HTTPRoute steers only the engine host.

The apply leg applies the lab `WAFPolicy`. The operator compiles rule `DX-LAB-001` and publishes the bundle.
The engine picks up the bundle. No restart happens.
The SQLi probe is a POST with a UNION probe in the query string. The engine answers 403.
The benign POST still passes: `defaultAction: pass` keeps the transparent forward.

The M9 leg carries a 5 s budget. The recorded smoke read 1174 ms. The M3 budget is 15 min
from clone to first enforced rule. The gate fails above either budget.

A broken policy fails at compile. The operator publishes no bundle. The engine keeps the loaded bundle.
The traffic shape does not change. Both pods stay Ready.

On OrbStack-provider Kubernetes, the NGF 2.x dataplane does not register.
`setup.sh` then installs the NGF 1.6.2 single-pod chart. The hop evidence stays the same.
